title: Chapel Ride
subject: Criminal Law & Procedure
stem:
Question ID: 14736_chapel_ride
Transformed from: 14736

After leaving a private Bible-study coffee night, Lydia stopped at a red traffic light in her home state. Paul opened the passenger door, got in, and pointed a gun at Lydia. Paul then directed Lydia to keep driving. They drove several miles, crossed into a neighboring state, and drove several more miles. When they reached an empty roadside lot near a small chapel, Paul ordered Lydia to pull over. Paul then took Lydia’s backpack, wallet, and cash, and ordered her out of the car. Paul drove off in Lydia’s car.

Paul is charged with kidnapping in the neighboring state, which has adopted the Model Penal Code.

Can Paul properly be convicted of kidnapping in the neighboring state?
call: Can Paul properly be convicted of kidnapping in the neighboring state?

choices.A: Yes, because Lydia was transported under threat of force in the neighboring state.
choices.B: Yes, because Lydia in effect paid a ransom for her release.
choices.C: No, because any kidnapping took place in Lydia’s home state.
choices.D: No, because the restraint was incidental to the robbery.

rightExplanation:
A is correct.

Gold Key: Under MPC-style kidnapping, forced removal a substantial distance from where the victim is found, or substantial confinement in isolation, can be kidnapping when done with a listed purpose such as facilitating a felony or flight. A long forced drive across a state line to a remote place is not merely incidental to the later robbery.

Silver Key: The answer array is a two-yes / two-no trap. First lock the call: charged in the neighboring state. Then ask whether the facts show forced movement there, not whether the robbery label feels more familiar.

Lydia was forced at gunpoint to keep driving after crossing into the neighboring state. That movement occurred in the charging state and was substantial enough to support kidnapping. The later robbery does not swallow the kidnapping because the forced ride was more than a brief restraint needed to take property.

wrongExplanations.B: “Ransom” is the wrong label. Lydia did not bargain for release or pay a ransom. Paul robbed her. The answer tries to convert stolen property into ransom, which the facts do not support.
wrongExplanations.C: The word any overclaims. The forced ride did not stop at the border. The facts place forced movement inside the neighboring state too. Gold Key: forced substantial removal in the charging state can support kidnapping there.
wrongExplanations.D: This is the main trap. Some restraint during a robbery can be too incidental to count as kidnapping. But this was not a momentary restraint while property was taken. It was a forced multi-mile ride across state lines to a remote place. Gold Key: long forced asportation to facilitate a felony is enough; the robbery does not erase the kidnapping.

c3.label: CUT B
c3.text: “Ransom” is a fact-label jump. The stem gives robbery, not ransom.

c3.label: CUT C
c3.text: “Any kidnapping took place in the home state” overclaims against the visible facts: the forced ride continued into the neighboring state.

c3.label: CLASH / CALL A vs D
c3.text: A says the forced movement in the neighboring state counts. D says robbery absorbs the restraint. Use the Gold Key. Multi-mile forced movement to a remote place is more than incidental.

studentScript: Cut ransom. Cut home-state-only after checking the charged-state movement. Then use the Gold Key: long forced movement to a remote place is not merely incidental to robbery. Pick A.

A.signal: A tracks the call: conviction in the neighboring state. It also uses the stem’s strongest fact: forced transport under threat there.
A.lawyer: Under MPC § 212.1, unlawful forced removal a substantial distance with a qualifying purpose supports kidnapping.

B.signal: The stem says Paul took Lydia’s wallet and cash. It does not say Lydia paid a ransom.
B.lawyer: Ransom is a separate kidnapping purpose; the correct route here is forced movement/felony facilitation, not ransom payment.

C.signal: The word 'any' fights the visible facts: the forced ride continued inside the neighboring state.
C.lawyer: Because substantial forced movement occurred in the neighboring state, that state may treat the movement there as kidnapping under the MPC-style rule.

D.signal: D uses the right trap word: incidental. But the facts show a long forced ride to a remote place.
D.lawyer: The incidental-restraint limitation does not defeat kidnapping where the movement is substantial and not merely part of the immediate taking of property.

goldKeys.statement: MPC-style kidnapping is satisfied by forced removal a substantial distance, or substantial isolation, with a listed purpose such as facilitating a felony or flight. A long forced drive to a remote place is not merely incidental to a robbery.
goldKeys.trigger: Victim is forced to travel miles, cross a state line, or go to a remote place before a robbery.
goldKeys.unlocks: Defeats the robbery-incidental trap in choice D and the home-state-only trap in choice C.

silverKeys.statement: When the call asks about conviction in a specific state, lock the state first. Then match the movement facts to that state before reading robbery labels.
silverKeys.trigger: Two answers say yes, two say no; one no-answer says the crime happened elsewhere.
silverKeys.unlocks: A/C location axis and A/D robbery-incidental trap.

remediation.title: Kidnapping vs robbery restraint
remediation.signal: Forced movement happens before or after a robbery.
remediation.studentMove: Ask whether the movement was substantial and separate enough from the immediate taking.
remediation.tinyRule: Brief restraint at the robbery scene may be incidental; a long forced ride to a remote place is not.
remediation.trap: Treating every robbery-related restraint as non-kidnapping.
